title: The last days of David Hume
gist: Marking 250 years since David Hume's death, the essay recounts how the great Scottish Enlightenment sceptic faced terminal illness with cheerful equanimity and no religious repentance, chronicled in his autobiography My Own Life and Adam Smith's controversial Letter to Strahan, and weighs this official account against a rival narrative of a fearful, gloomy death.

insights.claim: David Hume, the foremost thinker of the Scottish Enlightenment, is known for applying the scientific method to philosophical, political and historical problems and challenging entrenched positions in epistemology, constitutional theory and historiography.
insights.speaker: Max Skjönsberg
insights.so_what: Establishes Hume's method, empirical scepticism applied broadly, a durable model for interrogating received assumptions.
insights.quote: he is known for applying the scientific method to philosophical, political and historical problems

insights.claim: Hume named 'love of literary fame' as his life's ruling passion and became not just independent but 'opulent' from writing, with History of England royalties that 'exceeded anything formerly known in England'.
insights.speaker: Max Skjönsberg
insights.so_what: An early case of an author achieving wealth and independence purely through writing, a milestone in the economics of intellectual work.
insights.quote: he 'bec[a]me not only independent, but opulent' from his writing
insights.locator: He was also proud to point out

insights.claim: Hume's first book A Treatise of Human Nature, now considered a masterpiece, 'fell dead-born from the press', while his Political Discourses (1752) was his only immediate success, showing acclaim can lag far behind a work's eventual stature.
insights.speaker: Max Skjönsberg
insights.so_what: A reminder that initial market reception is a poor predictor of a work's long-run value, applicable well beyond publishing.
insights.quote: now considered a philosophical masterpiece, 'fell dead-born from the press'
insights.locator: We read about how his first book

insights.claim: Biographer James Harris argues Hume may have exaggerated his early failures in My Own Life to tell a more dramatic 'rags to riches' story and amplify his independent credentials, despite his rather comfortable life.
insights.speaker: Max Skjönsberg
insights.so_what: A caution that self-authored narratives, even by great minds, are curated for effect, relevant to reading any autobiography or founder story critically.
insights.quote: Hume may have misrepresented his rather comfortable life and tended to exaggerate some of his early failures
insights.locator: James Harris has argued in the standard modern biography

insights.claim: Hume met his terminal bowel cancer with striking equanimity, saying he had never suffered a moment's abatement of his spirits and was so detached from life that this final period was one he might most choose to live again.
insights.speaker: Max Skjönsberg
insights.so_what: The essay's central image: a model of serene, secular acceptance of death, offered as a template for a non-religious good death.
insights.quote: It is difficult to be more detached from life than I am at present.
insights.locator: My Own Life concludes with Hume's discovery

insights.claim: When Boswell pressed him in July 1776, Hume dismissed the afterlife, calling it 'a most unreasonable fancy that we should exist forever' and saying ceasing to exist after death was no scarier than not having existed before birth.
insights.speaker: Max Skjönsberg
insights.so_what: A crisp statement of Hume's consistent scepticism held even at death, the crux of why his passing became a test case.
insights.quote: ceasing to exist after death was not scarier than not having existed before birth
insights.locator: On 7 July 1776, Hume had been visited by James Boswell

insights.claim: Hume's death was a highly anticipated public event because many wanted to know whether a notorious infidel could die a philosophical death in a Christian age, staying true to his scepticism without anguish, or would repent.
insights.speaker: Max Skjönsberg
insights.so_what: Frames the stakes: Hume's deathbed became a public referendum on whether virtue and calm were possible without religion.
insights.quote: was it possible for a non-Christian to die a philosophical death in a Christian age?

insights.claim: Hume argued in The Natural History of Religion (1757) that religious belief arises partly from fear as people face life's uncertainties, and Rasmussen suggests Hume and Smith wanted to show one could live and die happily and virtuously without recourse to religion.
insights.speaker: Max Skjönsberg
insights.so_what: Links Hume's theory of religion-as-fear to the demonstrative purpose of his calm death, a coherent secular-ethics argument.
insights.quote: religious belief arises partly from fear as people face life's uncertainties and difficulties
insights.locator: Hume had argued in The Natural History of Religion

insights.claim: Hume and Adam Smith were in close contact for over 25 years, and from his sickbed Hume praised Smith's Wealth of Nations (1776) while noting 'If you were here at my Fireside, I should dispute some of your Principles.'
insights.speaker: Max Skjönsberg
insights.so_what: Documents the intimate intellectual exchange between two founders of modern economics and philosophy, context for the origins of classical economic thought.
insights.quote: If you were here at my Fireside, I should dispute some of your Principles.
insights.locator: Hume also kept revising his own writings

insights.claim: Anticipating David Ricardo, Hume argued from his sickbed that the rent of farms does not form part of the price of produce, which is 'determined altogether by the Quantity and the Demand'.
insights.speaker: Max Skjönsberg
insights.so_what: Shows Hume anticipating a core Ricardian price-theory insight, of interest to the intellectual history of economics.
insights.quote: the Price is determined altogether by the Quantity and the Demand

insights.claim: Smith summarised in Wealth of Nations Book Three that commerce and manufactures gradually introduced order, good government and individual liberty, crediting Hume as the only writer to have noticed this 'by far the most important' effect.
insights.speaker: Max Skjönsberg
insights.so_what: A foundational claim linking commerce to liberty and good governance, an intellectual root of the case for market-driven institutional development.
insights.quote: Commerce and manufactures gradually introduced order and good government, and with them, the liberty and security of individuals
insights.locator: One of the central claims of the work

insights.claim: Smith said his admiring Letter to Strahan eulogising the infidel Hume 'brought upon me ten times more abuse than the very violent attack I had made upon the whole commercial system of Great Britain' in Wealth of Nations.
insights.speaker: Max Skjönsberg
insights.so_what: A vivid measure of how much more dangerous religious dissent was than economic radicalism in the period, revealing the era's real taboos.
insights.quote: it 'brought upon me ten times more abuse than the very violent attack I had made upon the whole commercial system of Great Britain'
insights.locator: But since Hume had many detractors

insights.claim: Detractors refused to believe Hume's calm, with Samuel Johnson insisting 'It was not so, Sir. He had a vanity in being thought easy', and William Johnson Temple hoping the impious Hume would 'die the death of a Dog'.
insights.speaker: Max Skjönsberg
insights.so_what: Illustrates the fierce hostility a public figure's unrepentant secularism could provoke, a study in reputational conflict over worldview.
insights.quote: If he continue obstinate [he] will die the death of a Dog… Let him die then & be thrown into the ditch.

insights.claim: An alternative narrative, drawn from Zubia's 2024 book and 19th-century sources, holds Hume's housekeeper reported he was cheerful in company but often overwhelmed with unutterable gloom when alone, and afraid of being alone before his death.
insights.speaker: Max Skjönsberg
insights.so_what: A competing account used to argue religion is indispensable to a noble death, showing how the same life is enlisted for opposing ideological claims.
insights.quote: when alone he was often overwhelmed with unutterable gloom

insights.claim: The author concludes neither death narrative can be proven with certainty and both are partly mythical, but there is much more and more varied evidence supporting Hume and Smith's official account of a serene death.
insights.speaker: Max Skjönsberg
insights.so_what: A balanced evidentiary verdict favouring the serene account while acknowledging both are shaped by agenda, a model of weighing contested testimony.
insights.quote: there is much more, and a greater variety of, evidence on the side of Hume's and Smith's official account
insights.locator: As Zubia recognises, we cannot tell
